overview.text: Fluorine is a chemical element with symbol F and atomic number 9. On the Pauling scale, it has the highest electronegativity value, meaning its atoms strongly attract shared electrons in chemical bonds. At room temperature, pure fluorine is a very pale yellow-green, highly reactive gas. This hazardous elemental form is different from fluoride, the negatively charged ion found in many compounds. Fluoride compounds are used in toothpaste and some drinking water to help prevent tooth decay. In the mouth, fluoride helps replace minerals lost when acids attack teeth and makes enamel harder to dissolve, showing how fluorine-containing compounds can have useful roles even though elemental fluorine is dangerous.

key_facts.text: Fluorine is in group 17 and period 2 of the periodic table; its atomic number is 9.
Fluorine has an electronegativity of 3.98 on the Pauling scale—the highest value on that scale.
Elemental fluorine is a dangerously reactive gas; fluoride is the ion present in many compounds used in dental products.
Fluoride helps replace minerals lost from teeth and makes the outer enamel layer harder to dissolve.
Chemist Henri Moissan isolated fluorine in 1886 by electrolysis of potassium bifluoride dissolved in liquid hydrogen fluoride.
